\chapter{The Letters Ze and Toe}
\label{ch:ur-letters-ze-toe}
\hlchaptermodality{99}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write ze and toe, and find them in words I already say.}

Complete the last lesson of chapter 99: i can write ze and toe, and find them in words I already say.

\section[ze]{\ur{ز} (ze) — the letter that ends \ur{روز}}

\label{lesson:UR-W99-ze}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ur{ظ} and \ur{ئ} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ur{روز}} (\emph{roz}), \textquotedblleft{}every day\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ur{ز}}
\textbf{\ur{ز}} — \emph{ze}, the sound \emph{z}.

It ends \textbf{\ur{روز}} (\emph{roz}), \textquotedblleft{}every day\textquotedblright{}. You already write \textbf{\ur{ر}}, the short curve that drops below the line. \textbf{\ur{ز}} is the same curve with \textbf{one dot above} it. Like \textbf{\ur{ر}}, it never joins the letter after it.

\subsection*{Writing: \ur{ز}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/UR-W99-ze-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ur{ز} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: draw the independent ze downward
  \item \textbf{2.} continue curving to the left without lifting
  \item \textbf{3.} after one lift, place the dot above — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Zer o Zabar, Khe, ze, zāl, swād, and zwād, independent \ur{ز} calligraphic and handwriting animations and Ze instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ur{روز}} and point at \ur{ز} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ur{ز} three times, saying \emph{z} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ئ}, then \ur{ز}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{روز}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ur{ز}? (\textbf{ze}, \emph{z}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ur{روز}}, \emph{roz}, \textquotedblleft{}every day\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[toe]{\ur{ط} (toe) — the letter that opens \ur{طرف}}

\label{lesson:UR-W99-toe}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ur{ئ} and \ur{ز} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ur{طرف}} (\emph{taraf}), \textquotedblleft{}a side, a direction\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ur{ط}}
\textbf{\ur{ط}} — \emph{toe}, a plain \emph{t} sound, the same as \textbf{\ur{ت}}.

It opens \textbf{\ur{طرف}} (\emph{taraf}), \textquotedblleft{}a side, a direction\textquotedblright{}. You already write \textbf{\ur{ظ}}: a flat loop on the line with a tall upright stroke. \textbf{\ur{ط}} is that shape with \textbf{no dot}. Urdu keeps it for words that came from Arabic.

\subsection*{Writing: \ur{ط}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/UR-W99-toe-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ur{ط} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: draw the independent to'e-series loop
  \item \textbf{2.} continue through its leftward finish without lifting
  \item \textbf{3.} after one lift, draw the tall upright — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Zer o Zabar, To’e, zo’e, se, zhe, and ġhain, independent \ur{ط} handwriting animation and To’e instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ur{طرف}} and point at \ur{ط} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ur{ط} three times, saying \emph{t} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ز}, then \ur{ط}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{طرف}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ur{ط}? (\textbf{toe}, \emph{t}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ur{طرف}}, \emph{taraf}, \textquotedblleft{}a side, a direction\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
